lead: Paul asks a divided community to welcome one another, because Christ came to confirm God's promises to Israel and to bring the nations to praise. He ends with “the root of Jesse” from Isaiah. The Gospel takes the Holy Family back from Egypt to an unknown village, where the promised one will be called a Nazorean. Both readings show God keeping his word in unexpected ways.

set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome in the later 50s, probably from Corinth. He did not found that Church. It seems to have had believers of both Jewish and Gentile background, who differed about food and holy days. Chapters 14 and 15 address this tension, speaking of the “weak” and the “strong”. Today's passage draws it together: both groups are one in Christ, and Scripture has always foreseen it.
str: v. 7: the command: welcome one another, as Christ has welcomed you.
vv. 8–9a: Christ served the circumcised for God's truth, and the Gentiles for God's mercy.
vv. 9b–12: four quotations: Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1, Isaiah 11:10.
v. 13: a closing blessing: the God of hope.
kw: To take someone to oneself, to receive into one's home and circle. The word opened this section (14:1), and God is its subject there too (14:3).
Jesus is a Jew who served his own people, to keep God's word to their ancestors. Paul says this to Gentile Christians, so that they will not forget it.
The shoot from David's family (Isaiah 11:1, 10). Today's Gospel may echo the same chapter.
vv: Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
The welcome is measured by Christ's welcome, not by how much we like one another.
The root of Jesse shall come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope.
Paul's chain of texts draws on the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms: all of Scripture is singing the same song.
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Hope, in Paul, is not an optimistic temperament. It comes from God, and it grows in believing.
ch: The Catechism quotes this blessing as the prayer of hope (CCC 2657) and describes hope as the virtue by which we rely not on our own strength but on the help of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). The welcome Paul asks for marks the Church, which is one people gathered from all nations (CCC 831).

r.h: He will be called a Nazorean
set: Herod the Great died about 4 BC, and Augustus divided his kingdom among his sons. Archelaus received Judea. According to Josephus, he began his reign with a harsh crackdown at Passover in which many died, and he was finally deposed and banished in AD 6. Herod Antipas received Galilee. So Joseph's fear was reasonable. Nazareth was a small village, not mentioned in the Old Testament, in a region that Judeans did not much regard (compare John 1:46).
str: vv. 19–20: the dream in Egypt: go back to the land of Israel.
v. 22: fear of Archelaus, and a second warning.
kw: Matthew hears the place name in this title. Two Old Testament words are often suggested: nēṣer, the “branch” from Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), and nāzîr, one consecrated to God, as Samson was (Judges 13:5). No one is sure which Matthew had in mind, and he may be thinking of both.
Literally “take along with you”. Joseph is told to take “the child and his mother”, the same phrase that recurs through this chapter (2:13, 14, 20, 21).
vv: Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life are dead.
This echoes God's word to Moses: “all those who were seeking your life are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Matthew shows Jesus reliving Israel's story and the story of Moses.
Then Joseph got up, took the child and his mother, and went to the land of Israel.
Joseph says nothing in this Gospel. He is told and he does, in almost the same words.
There he made his home in a town called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, “He will be called a Nazorean.”

No Old Testament verse has these exact words. The Greek says “through the prophets”, in the plural (the POC has the singular), which suggests a general sense of prophecy and not one text. St Jerome draws this very conclusion: Matthew takes the sense of the Scriptures and not their words (in substance).
ch: The Catechism sees in the return from Egypt the Exodus story, with Jesus as the definitive liberator (CCC 530), and it treats the years at Nazareth as Jesus' sharing in the daily life of most people (CCC 531–533). Pope Francis, in Patris Corde 3, draws from Joseph's dreams the portrait of an obedient father, who at each step does as he is told.

study: Who is the person in my parish or family that I find it hardest to “welcome”? What would Christ's welcome look like toward them?
Joseph acted at once on a word he could only half understand. What small step of obedience is before me now?
